records.answer: The Agent Gateway registers A2A agents with an agent ID, set in the Admin UI, the /v1/agents API or config.yaml. Calls can carry an X-LiteLLM-Agent-Id header for spend attribution, and JWT auth can bind tokens to registered agents. Agent records hold a name, URL, protocol version and agent card fields, but the docs do not describe a linked owner or release record.
records.gaps: No documented owner or release linkage on the agent record. Attribution via X-LiteLLM-Agent-Id is a caller-supplied header. Workload identity for agents that call LiteLLM depends on the virtual key they hold.
records.options: Issue one virtual key per agent with owner metadata, and test whether a key can spoof another agent's X-LiteLLM-Agent-Id header.

records.answer: Clients authenticate with virtual keys while provider and MCP credentials stay in the gateway. Keys can be scoped to models, given a duration, blocked and unblocked, and capped by upperbound parameters. Key regeneration with a grace period, scheduled auto-rotation and secret manager integration (AWS, Azure, Google, HashiCorp Vault, CyberArk) require an Enterprise licence.
records.gaps: Rotation and secret manager storage need an Enterprise licence. Storing virtual keys in a secret manager is off by default. Keeping provider secrets out of model context depends on clients not passing them through.
records.options: Enable rotation_interval and store_virtual_keys under an Enterprise licence, and confirm a blocked or expired key is rejected across all proxy instances.

records.answer: For MCP servers, auth_type oauth2_token_exchange exchanges the caller's bearer token at the identity provider (RFC 8693, or Entra jwt-bearer OBO) and forwards only the scoped token. Tokens are cached per subject token and server, so users get separate tokens. JWT auth can set the end-user ID from a verified claim, which overrides any request value.
records.gaps: The A2A gateway does not automatically forward the caller's virtual key or end-user ID to backend agents. JWT auth needs an Enterprise licence.
records.options: Use OBO for MCP servers that accept identity provider tokens, and test that a request without a subject token is refused rather than falling back to a shared credential.

records.answer: The A2A gateway authenticates callers with a LiteLLM virtual key and checks whether the key and its team may invoke the target agent, returning 403 otherwise. Agents can require a trace ID on inbound calls. The docs do not describe agent-to-agent trust boundaries or mutual authentication between agents.
records.gaps: No rules on which agents may call which other agents. Caller identity is not forwarded to the backend agent.
records.options: Give each calling agent its own key restricted to permitted target agents, and authenticate the gateway to backend agents at the agent runtime.

records.answer: LiteLLM is a network gateway and does not run on or control the agent's local host. Checked the MCP, A2A, guardrail and tool policy docs for local file, process or shell controls and found none.
records.gaps: No control over local host actions.
records.options: Use the agent harness or endpoint sandbox for local scopes.

records.answer: MCP Permission Management assigns allowed servers at key, team, end user, agent, internal user and organisation level, intersecting the lists so the most restrictive wins. allowed_tools, disallowed_tools and allowed_params restrict tools and their parameters, with 403 on violation. A2A agent access and model access are scoped per key and team in the same way.
records.gaps: Servers marked allow_all_keys bypass per-key grants. Keys with an empty list inherit the team list unless require_key_mcp_access_defined is set.
records.options: Set require_key_mcp_access_defined, avoid allow_all_keys for sensitive servers, and test parameter restrictions with crafted tool calls.

records.answer: On the MCP gateway, require_approval controls whether the proxy runs tool calls itself. Unless it is set to never, tool calls are returned to the client for review. The approval decision, its binding to the exact call and replay handling sit with the client application.
records.gaps: No gateway-side approval record, approver identity, denial handling or replay protection is documented.
records.options: Implement approval in the client or harness and log approver identity alongside the LiteLLM call ID.

records.answer: Keys, teams, users, agents, MCP servers and models are created, updated, blocked and deleted through the Admin UI, API or config.yaml. key_generation_settings, upperbound parameters and custom key policy hooks restrict who can create keys and with what limits. Organisation and team admin roles and team member permissions are Premium features under an Enterprise licence.
records.gaps: No approval step for agent creation. Fine-grained RBAC needs an Enterprise licence. Config-defined agents need a restart to change.
records.options: Manage agents and keys through config.yaml or Terraform under change control, and enable audit logs to record changes.

records.answer: LiteLLM does not sequence agent workflows. It retries model calls, falls back across model groups and cools down unhealthy deployments. For agents it caps iterations and spend per session and offers an admin-fired kill switch webhook to stop an agent runtime.
records.gaps: No workflow definition, task delegation or recovery of agent state. Retries apply per model call only.
records.options: Use an orchestration framework for sequencing and rely on LiteLLM for per-call retry and session caps.

records.answer: Each model name maps to explicit provider deployments with API base, credentials and per-deployment rpm limits, managed in config.yaml or the model API. Timeouts, context window pre-call checks and region_name filtering for routing are configurable. LiteLLM routes to providers and does not host model weights.
records.gaps: Data handling at the provider depends on provider terms. Region filtering needs enable_pre_call_checks.
records.options: Pin deployments to provider model versions and regions, and test that fallbacks respect region and access rules (enforce_fallback_model_access).

records.answer: LiteLLM provides no code interpreter or sandboxed host for agents. Checked the proxy, MCP and A2A docs.
records.gaps: Execution environment is out of scope.
records.options: Use a separate sandbox runtime.

records.answer: LiteLLM uses session IDs (x-litellm-trace-id) to count iterations and spend, with counters expiring after an hour. It does not store session state for agents. Checked the A2A and iteration budget docs.
records.gaps: No session memory store, access control or resumption.
records.options: Keep session state in the agent framework.

records.answer: LiteLLM proxies tool calls to MCP servers and can run them when require_approval is never, but it is not an agent harness. Checked the MCP docs.
records.gaps: No harness for local tool execution.
records.options: Use an agent framework or coding agent harness.

records.answer: Spend logs can store prompts and responses when store_prompts_in_spend_logs is on, but this is logging, not agent memory. No long-term memory feature is documented.
records.gaps: No persistent agent memory.
records.options: Use a memory store in the agent framework.

records.answer: Virtual keys enforce allowed models, budgets, TPM, RPM and parallel limits per key, user, team, organisation, agent and customer, with per-model limits. Guardrails run pre_call, during_call and post_call, including built-in prompt injection detection by similarity or LLM check and third-party providers such as Lakera and Bedrock. Per key, team and model guardrail control requires an Enterprise licence.
records.gaps: Budgets need Postgres and fail open without it. Rate limits need Redis to be shared across instances. Several named guardrail integrations need an Enterprise licence.
records.options: Run Postgres and Redis, set default_on guardrails, and test injection detection with a known attack set.

records.answer: The MCP gateway enforces allowed servers, tools and tool parameters per key, team, agent and organisation, per-server rate limits and per-server auth config (OAuth, OBO, API key, SigV4). MCP guardrails run pre_mcp_call on arguments and on tool descriptions during discovery, and post_mcp_call on results. Tool Policies classify tools seen in traffic as trusted, untrusted or blocked and block trust-chain violations.
records.gaps: General internet egress for agents is not controlled. Tool Policy overrides per team or key only block.
records.options: Route all agent tool traffic through the MCP gateway and control other egress at the network layer.

records.answer: Presidio guardrails mask or block PII entities per entity type on input, output and MCP calls, with confidence thresholds. Secret detection and redaction is an Enterprise guardrail. The docs reviewed do not describe enforcement of retrieval permissions per user or agent.
records.gaps: No retrieval-level authorisation documented in the pages reviewed. Presidio runs as separate containers.
records.options: Deploy Presidio with entity rules per team, and test masking on streaming and MCP results.

records.answer: The A2A gateway restricts which agents a key or team may invoke, using direct grants and agent access groups, and hides other agents from the registry listing. Agents can require trace IDs. It does not define allowed agent pairs or validate message schemas.
records.gaps: No pair-level rules or schema enforcement for A2A messages.
records.options: Assign each agent its own key limited to the agents it may call.

records.answer: The Logs tab shows requests and responses when prompt storage is on, but there is no output review or sign-off workflow. Checked the logging, A2A and MCP docs.
records.gaps: No human review queue for outputs.
records.options: Export logs to an evaluation or review tool such as Langfuse.

records.answer: No behavioural baselining or anomaly detection of agent behaviour is documented. Alerting covers slow, hanging and failed calls and budget thresholds.
records.gaps: No behavioural monitoring.
records.options: Send logs to an observability or security platform for behavioural analysis.

records.answer: Spend is tracked automatically per key, user, team, tag, customer, model and agent, with tokens and cost in spend logs, Prometheus and the Usage UI. Spend reports by team, customer or key (Enterprise) support chargeback. Soft budget alerts and weekly or monthly spend reports go to Slack or Teams.
records.gaps: Covers token cost only. No infrastructure, labour, savings or yield measures.
records.options: Join LiteLLM spend exports with business output data elsewhere.

records.answer: Prometheus metrics cover end-to-end and provider latency, time to first token, in-flight requests, failures, deployment health state, cooldowns and fallbacks, with maintained Grafana dashboards. Alerting reports hanging, slow and failed calls, model outages and database failures. Region outage alerting is an Enterprise feature.
records.gaps: Detection is threshold based. No statistical anomaly detection is documented.
records.options: Build anomaly rules on the Prometheus metrics in the monitoring stack.

records.answer: The gateway returns each caller only the MCP tools and agents it may use, and the dashboard shows MCP servers and permissions per entity. Tool Policies keeps a registry of tools observed in traffic. AI Hub lists published models, agents and MCP servers.
records.gaps: No consolidated map of an agent's reach across models, tools and agents.
records.options: Query key, team and MCP permission APIs to build a reach view per agent key.

records.answer: Audit logs (Enterprise) record create, update, delete and regenerate actions on keys, teams, users and models with actor, hashed key, before and after values, and can be exported to S3. Spend logs record each request with key, user and team, and can store prompts and responses. The docs make no tamper-resistance claim.
records.gaps: No immutability or integrity checks. Before v1.84.0 the LiteLLM-Changed-By header could rewrite attribution. Admins can turn audit logs off. Reasoning is not captured.
records.options: Export audit logs to write-once S3 storage and confirm allow_litellm_changed_by_header is off.

records.answer: Logging callbacks send a standard payload with call ID, key, user and team to OpenTelemetry, Datadog, S3 and others. Message logging can be turned off or redacted per request, and key details can be redacted. Guardrail results and MCP tool drift alerts are emitted.
records.gaps: No security detections or response ownership. Per-team logging needs an Enterprise licence.
records.options: Forward logs to a SIEM and build detections on guardrail blocks and permission denials.

records.answer: LiteLLM routes to hosted providers and does not inspect model files or produce lineage or AI BoM records. Checked model management docs.
records.gaps: Out of scope.
records.options: Use a model scanning or AI BoM tool.

records.answer: No assurance of inference or tool execution containers or hosts is documented. LiteLLM is self-hosted and its own runtime hardening is the deployer's task.
records.gaps: Out of scope.
records.options: Apply container and host security tooling to the proxy and MCP servers.

records.answer: MCP server submissions are held in pending_review until an admin approves them. Tool pinning freezes a server's tool names, descriptions and schemas and alerts on drift. pre_mcp_call guardrails scan tool descriptions during discovery and hide blocked tools.
records.gaps: No SBOM or code scanning of MCP servers, CLIs or skills.
records.options: Pin tool lists for all servers and add code scanning in the MCP server build pipeline.

records.answer: Tool pinning detects upstream changes to tool names, descriptions and schemas, which covers some tool metadata poisoning. Description scanning on discovery can block suspect tools. New server names must follow SEP-986.
records.gaps: No checks for name squatting or package compromise in third-party registries.
records.options: Combine pinning with an external MCP scanner before submission.

records.answer: No data or feature store governance is documented. Checked the guardrail and logging docs.
records.gaps: Out of scope.
records.options: Use data platform governance tools.

records.answer: LiteLLM only sees traffic routed through it. Tool Policies discovers tools in that traffic, but there is no discovery of AI use that bypasses the gateway.
records.gaps: No shadow AI discovery.
records.options: Use network or endpoint discovery tools and force egress to providers through the gateway.

records.answer: No automated adversarial testing feature is documented. Checked guardrail and enterprise docs.
records.gaps: Out of scope.
records.options: Run a red-teaming tool against the gateway endpoints.

records.answer: The gateway keeps registries of models, A2A agents, MCP servers and observed tools, with model_info metadata and agent card fields. AI Hub publishes selected models, agents and MCP servers to a discovery page and API.
records.gaps: No software component records. Inventory covers only assets registered in the gateway.
records.options: Export registry APIs into a central asset inventory.

records.answer: Team members submit MCP servers with a team-scoped key and admins approve or reject them with review notes through the UI or API. Models and agents are added directly by admins without a submission step.
records.gaps: Approval workflow covers MCP servers only. Admin keys bypass it.
records.options: Restrict admin keys and route model and agent changes through an external change process.

records.answer: Prometheus exposes guardrail errors, admission rejections and budget headroom. Response headers report which policies and guardrails applied, and the Policies Test tab shows which apply to a team, key or model.
records.gaps: No control coverage or risk register view.
records.options: Build a dashboard from guardrail and permission metrics.

records.answer: Guardrail Policies (beta) group guardrails, inherit from parent policies and attach globally or to teams, keys, models or tags, managed in config.yaml or the dashboard. Team and key attachments need an Enterprise licence.
records.gaps: No policy ownership, versioning, publication or review cycle documented. Feature is beta.
records.options: Keep policy config in version control with review.

records.answer: No lifecycle stages from proposal to retirement for models, agents or use cases are documented.
records.gaps: Out of scope.
records.options: Use a governance platform.

records.answer: Keys belong to a user or team, and key metadata and model_info fields can hold an owner. Spend is attributed to key owners and teams.
records.gaps: Owner fields are free-form metadata. No owner maintenance or review for agents and tools.
records.options: Enforce owner metadata through custom key policy hooks.

records.answer: No use case risk assessment or classification feature is documented.
records.gaps: Out of scope.
records.options: Use a governance platform.

records.answer: Prompt Management (beta) versions prompts on each save and lets calls pin a prompt_version. Audit logs record changes to keys, teams, users and models with before and after values. Tool pinning detects tool changes.
records.gaps: No approval step for changes. Prompt rollback is by re-saving an older version.
records.options: Use config.yaml in Git with pull request review for model, policy and permission changes.

records.answer: No policy exception register is documented. temp_budget_increase with an expiry raises a key budget temporarily, which is a spend override, not an exception record.
records.gaps: No exception recording, approval or review.
records.options: Track exceptions outside the gateway.

records.answer: Spend log retention is set by maximum_spend_logs_retention_period with a cleanup job, without an Enterprise licence. Message logging can be turned off or redacted, and Presidio can mask logged data only. region_name filtering limits routing to a region.
records.gaps: With no retention setting nothing is deleted. Retention at providers and logging destinations is outside LiteLLM.
records.options: Set retention, turn off message logging where not needed, and align callback destination retention.

records.answer: Audit logs and spend logs can be exported to S3 and logging platforms as evidence. The enterprise page states LiteLLM is SOC 2 Type II audited with the report in its Trust Center.
records.gaps: No mapping of controls to requirements. The SOC 2 report covers the vendor, not a self-hosted deployment.
records.options: Map exported logs to control requirements in a GRC tool.

records.answer: External MCP servers go through submission and approval, and rejecting an active server removes it from the registry. Models and providers are added and deleted by admins.
records.gaps: No periodic reassessment or approval for model providers.
records.options: Schedule review of registered MCP servers and providers outside the gateway.

records.answer: Callers are identified as AI Consumers, resolved by an AI Auth Strategy from an API key or an OIDC token claim. Kong Identity issues client credentials whose client ID becomes the consumer's custom_id, giving a machine identity for an agent. Upstream agents are registered as AI Agent entities with an immutable name.
records.gaps: No documented link from a consumer identity to an owner, runtime or release version. Identity is per gateway caller, not a workload attestation.
records.options: Use labels and naming conventions to carry owner and release, or pair with a workload identity system such as SPIFFE and map its claims to consumers.

records.answer: Provider and upstream credentials are held in AI Vaults (HashiCorp Vault, AWS, GCP, Azure, CyberArk Conjur or the write-only Konnect Config Store) and resolved by reference at request time, so callers never see the provider key. The AI MCP OAuth2 plugin strips the caller's token before forwarding by default and can exchange it for a different token, cached until its expiry. Changelog 2.2.0 adds Token Vault support...
records.gaps: Rotation is left to the backing vault and cache settings. Token Vault has a changelog entry but no dedicated documentation page was found. Token exchange is Enterprise tier.
records.options: Use a dynamic secrets backend with short cache TTLs and test revocation propagation through the gateway cache grace period.

records.answer: The AI MCP OAuth2 plugin validates the user's token, then can exchange it as the subject token (with an optional actor token) for a token scoped to the upstream MCP server. It can also forward token claims, including nested claims, to the upstream as headers.
records.gaps: Documented for MCP traffic only. LLM and A2A delegation is not described. Requires Kong Gateway 3.14 or later and the AI Gateway Enterprise tier.
records.options: Test exchange against the target IdP (for example Okta, which needs the actor token) and confirm the downstream audit shows the original user.

records.answer: AI Agent entities of type a2a proxy A2A traffic and require callers to authenticate through an AI Auth Strategy (key-auth or OIDC). ACLs allow or deny AI Consumers, consumer groups or authenticated groups before traffic reaches the upstream agent, and the gateway can sign upstream requests with AWS SigV4.
records.gaps: Access is controlled at the agent level, not per skill. Upstream authentication beyond SigV4 is not described. The getting-started guide configures no authentication.
records.options: Configure OIDC auth strategies on every agent and test that a denied consumer gets 403 for agent card and message calls.

records.answer: Kong AI Gateway mediates network traffic and does not control actions an agent takes on its local host.
records.gaps: Checked the AI Gateway overview and entity pages. No local host controls.
records.options: Use the agent runtime or endpoint controls for local scopes.

records.answer: AI MCP Server entities convert REST APIs to MCP tools or proxy upstream MCP servers, validate tool calls against OpenAPI or JSON Schema parameters, enforce per-consumer tool ACLs and inbound OAuth2, and run attached rate limiting and logging policies. records.gaps: AI Guardrails are listed as not supported on MCP traffic, so tool calls and results are not injection screened. Annotations for destructive tools are hints only. No general internet egress allow list is described.

records.answer: AI PII Sanitizer masks PII in requests and responses through a separate PII service, with placeholder or synthetic replacement and custom regex patterns. records.gaps: Retrieval control covers only the gateway's own RAG Injector vector store. The RAG page gives conflicting examples on default ACL behaviour. PII service must be deployed separately.

packages.name: AI use discovery and safe-use boundaries
packages.prerequisite: Sponsor authorises bounded discovery and assigns owners to unknowns.
packages.completion_evidence: A reconciled sample inventory, permitted-use guidance and risk triage record, with unknown coverage visible.
packages.do_not_progress_if: No person accepts responsibility for the use or its data boundary.

packages.name: Controlled assistance and task adoption
packages.prerequisite: Approved tools and tasks, support contact and authorised sources exist.
packages.completion_evidence: Users demonstrate safe task completion and escalation, with baseline effort and rework recorded.
packages.do_not_progress_if: Users cannot identify unacceptable outputs or sensitive input restrictions.

packages.name: Measured pilot and go or stop evidence
packages.prerequisite: Representative authorised data, task owner, test environment and agreed acceptance criteria.
packages.completion_evidence: Baseline comparison includes failure cases, harms, review effort and documented release recommendation.
packages.do_not_progress_if: Material risk, permission or evidence gaps remain without accountable acceptance.

packages.name: Production readiness and service support
packages.prerequisite: A pilot has accepted task evidence and operational ownership.
packages.completion_evidence: End-to-end exception, denial, fallback, support and change exercises meet the client's task requirements.
packages.do_not_progress_if: The service cannot be stopped, supported or recovered by authorised staff.

packages.name: Shared controls and accountable enterprise scale
packages.prerequisite: Several uses have functioning local owners, service evidence and shared-platform visibility.
packages.completion_evidence: Shared dependencies, costs and exceptions reconcile to local use cases with exercised escalation and failure boundaries.
packages.do_not_progress_if: Central approval replaces local accountability or supplier concentration lacks a credible contingency.

packages.name: Operating assurance, optimisation and replacement
packages.prerequisite: Operating outcomes, failures, changes and costs are measurable with sufficient history.
packages.completion_evidence: Independent challenge and regression evidence support an improvement, replacement or retirement decision.
packages.do_not_progress_if: An optimisation improves one measure while breaching accepted harm, permission or service limits.

concerns.concern: How does agent-to-agent (A2A) authorisation work, and how do we stop one agent acting with another agent's permissions?
concerns.summary: Your Okta agent identities from c4-1 are the strongest base, because Okta lets one agent call another under the target's identity with scoped tokens and enforces this at token issuance. Claude Code has no cryptographic agent authentication for agent-to-agent traffic, and Wiz and Purview do not address the channel, so nothing in your stack inspects messages on the wire. To stop one agent borrowing another's permissions, give every agent its own identity, restrict allowed callers per target, and add a gateway if you need message-path enforcement.

Test a two-agent chain in Okta and confirm the System Log shows both identities, then test a caller with no connection is refused.
Test multi-hop delegation explicitly, since Okta does not describe chains beyond one hop.
Keep Claude Code agent teams disabled in managed settings unless needed, and decide whether cross-boundary agent traffic needs an external A2A gateway.

claims.text: Okta's Connect to another AI agent resource connection lets one agent call another under the target's identity through an authorisation server and audience with allowed scopes. This is the in-stack mechanism that keeps a caller from simply reusing the callee's permissions.

Okta's agent-to-agent connections define which agents may call which, but enforcement happens at token issuance. There is no inline gateway for A2A traffic and no message schema enforcement described, so support is partial.

Okta Agent Gateway exchanges the agent token for downstream tokens on behalf of the user, and a linked app restricts an agent to acting for users currently signed in. Downstream apps must implement the ID-JAG grant, and delegation chains beyond one hop are not described.

Claude Code agent teams pass messages through local mailbox files between sessions of the same user on one machine. There is no cryptographic authentication of agents or trust boundary definition, and the feature is experimental and off by default, so support is partial.

Claude Code's RFC 8693 act chain exists only in self-hosted environments, and Anthropic advises treating the session token as weaker than a direct login. Local sessions pass the developer's own credentials rather than a delegated, attenuated token.

AWS AgentCore Runtime supports A2A communication, but the assessment notes that discovery and protocol interoperability do not confer authority. Peer endpoints should be pinned and caller identity verified.

AWS Gateway documents passthrough targets including A2A, but protocol support alone does not prove pairwise delegation restrictions. Peers need authenticating and unapproved agent pairs denying, and no deployed configuration was tested.

Alternative: Kong AI Gateway AI Agent entities enforce which consumers or groups may call each agent and detect A2A JSON-RPC bindings. It has no skill-level ACLs, does not validate payloads beyond envelope detection, and allowed pairs depend on each calling agent having its own consumer identity.

Alternative: Microsoft Entra Agent ID uses Conditional Access scoped by agent identity or blueprint to decide which agents get tokens for a callee, and risk policies can block risky agents. Enforcement is at token issuance, not on the message path.

Alternative: Ping Identity Agent Privilege places remote agents behind an AI gateway with policy on which operations agents can use, and AI Guard inspects agent-to-agent traffic. A broader allowed-pairs matrix is not described.

concerns.concern: What gateway do we need in front of models and MCP tools?
concerns.summary: The client's stack already has partial gateway coverage, but no single product covers both models and MCP tools. Claude Code's own gateway and AWS Gateway are the main model and tool candidates, while Okta covers MCP traffic only and Wiz and Purview do not act as gateways. Gaps remain in prompt injection screening, rate limits and schema validation, so the client needs a model gateway with fail-closed settings plus a content-aware tool gateway.
next_steps: Set enforcement.fail_closed_on_error on the Claude apps gateway and confirm that spend caps return 429 when Postgres is unavailable.
Route all inference through the configured AWS Gateway endpoint and test failover and per-model quotas.
Run denial tests against AWS Gateway for unknown tools and alternate egress paths, and allow only reviewed schemas and destinations.
Choose a content-aware MCP gateway for rate limits, schema validation and injection screening, and confirm Okta Agent Gateway GA status for the tenant.

claims.text: Claude Code's self-hosted Claude apps gateway signs users in with the corporate IdP, enforces model access per IdP group, routes and fails over between Bedrock, Google Cloud, Foundry and the Anthropic API, and caps spend per user, group or organisation.

The Claude apps gateway has no documented prompt injection screening, spend enforcement fails open by default if Postgres is unavailable, and caps are USD estimates rather than token rate limits. Setting enforcement.fail_closed_on_error is the suggested fix.
AWS Gateway documents model-based routing across providers, but per-model quotas and failover semantics need verification on the selected route, and no deployed configuration was tested.

Claude Code enforces tool policy on the client side through permission rules, managed MCP allowlists, PreToolUse hooks and sandbox egress allowlists. This is not a separate gateway and has no tool quotas, rate limits or schema validation policy.
AWS Gateway exposes APIs and MCP tools with authentication, and policy checks tool calls. Unknown tools and alternate egress paths still need denial tests.

Okta Agent Gateway sits between agents and remote MCP servers, validates tokens, exposes only admin-selected tools and injects downstream credentials. It documents no rate limits, schema validation or injection screening, covers MCP only, and GA was stated for Q3.
Okta's gateway does not route, quota or screen model calls, so it does not serve as the model gateway.
Wiz has no model gateway. It checks that provider guardrails are enabled and flags AI endpoints not protected by Cloudflare, but enforcement at the edge is done by Cloudflare.
Purview offers only partial coverage. It has no model routing, quota or rate limits, and its prompt blocking is in preview.
Purview covers web search and AI site egress only, with no per-agent tool allow lists, schema checks or rate limits for tools.

concerns.concern: Can prompts, outputs and agent memory stay in Australia?
concerns.summary: The records do not confirm that prompts, outputs and agent memory can stay in Australia. Claude Code says residency follows the chosen provider or a gateway routing inference through the customer's cloud, and AWS residency needs service-specific validation. Purview does not address residency, and Wiz and Okta do not cover it.

Ask Microsoft for written confirmation of where Purview-retained AI interaction copies are stored.

claims.text: Claude Code residency follows the chosen provider, or a gateway that routes inference through the customer's cloud. Support is partial and unverified, so the required region has to be selected and confirmed.

Claude Code auto memory has no documented retention limit, and feedback transcripts are kept for 5 years when users submit them. Both are gaps for a residency position unless disabled in managed settings.
Claude Code auto memory is machine-local plaintext with no documented expiry. It can be disabled with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY where retention must be controlled.

Claude Code local session transcripts sit under the user's home directory and are retained for 30 days by default. Cloud session transcripts are stored by Anthropic, so location of that copy is not settled by these records.

Claude Code allows restricting API providers with allowedProviders and pinning model IDs on Bedrock, Google Cloud and Foundry. This can be used to keep inference on a chosen cloud, but organisation-level server-side model controls do not reach third-party cloud providers.
For AWS AgentCore memory, retention, downstream deletion and residency need service-specific validation. No Region or deployed configuration was tested, so Australian residency is not confirmed.
AWS Bedrock model, feature and Region availability must be checked for the selected deployment. The exact model identifier and supported Region should be recorded.
Purview retention policies can retain or delete prompts and responses, but residency is not addressed on the reviewed pages. Deletion can take up to about 16 days.
AWS AgentCore Memory persists events across sessions, which is the store where agent memory residency would need to be traced. Namespace access, correction and deletion should be tested.

concerns.concern: How do we make a person approve an agent action before it runs, with evidence of who approved it?
concerns.summary: Your stack can force a human approval before an agent action, but it only partly proves who approved it. Claude Code and Auth0 CIBA are the strongest routes, and each decision can be logged with a user identity, though neither is documented as tamper-evident. The audit capability you already have (c7-1) is partial, so approval evidence would need to be exported to write-once storage and tested.
next_steps: Set permissions.defaultMode or disableAutoMode in Claude Code managed settings so a human prompt is retained where approval is required.
Export Claude Code tool_decision events to write-once storage and confirm each carries the approving user's identity.
Pilot Auth0 CIBA with RAR for one high-risk agent action and test denial, expiry and replay behaviour.
Check with your Airia contact for the audit log schema and whether a receipt can be verified independently before considering it.

claims.text: Claude Code in Manual mode shows the exact command or edit and asks before running it. Unmatched commands fail closed to a prompt, and each decision is emitted as a tool_decision event with its source.

Claude Code gaps: Auto mode, the default in recent versions, replaces most human prompts with a classifier, and always-allow grants persist per repository. The approver is the local user with no separate authorisation check, so approval is not tied to a named authorised approver.

Auth0 for AI Agents offers CIBA with RAR, so an agent waits for a user to approve an action on a separate device with Guardian push showing the details. This is partial support, and CIBA needs an Auth0 Enterprise plan or add-on.
Okta workforce approval routing applies to access requests for agent-linked apps, not individual agent actions. Binding message, expiry and replay handling are not described on the page read.

Bedrock action groups support user confirmation and returning control to the application. Approval identity, expiry and replay protection need application tests, and no deployed configuration was tested.
Wiz has no approval step for actions an AI agent proposes. Its Workflows approval covers only Wiz's own containment actions, so it cannot supply this control.
Claude Code telemetry carries tool decisions with session and user attributes, which can serve as approval evidence. There is no tamper-evident ledger and local transcripts are editable by the user.

The Okta System Log records agent token exchanges and Agent Gateway logs every tool call. Tamper evidence, log schema and retention are not described on the pages read, and inputs and outputs are not captured.

Alternative if tamper-evident approval records are required: Airia release notes describe an AI Gateway feed with tamper-evident receipts covering identity, session, tool call, policy decision and outcome. The audit documentation requires a login and was not read, and human approval is not described.
